question:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows.

"Government offices in India have, for decades, run on paper. A single land record, a pension file or a court exhibit would travel from desk to desk in a cloth-bound bundle, and its safety depended entirely on the diligence of the clerk who carried it. The shift to electronic records was therefore welcomed as an unqualified good. Files could now be retrieved in seconds, copied without loss, and shared across districts at negligible cost.

Yet the transition has produced a difficulty that few anticipated. Paper decays slowly and predictably; a ledger written in 1890 can still be read today by anyone who knows the script. Digital records, by contrast, decay in a manner that is sudden and total. A file written in a word processor that is no longer sold may become unreadable within fifteen years, not because the storage medium has failed, but because no surviving program can interpret its format. Archivists call this problem format obsolescence, and it has already cost several departments their earliest computerised records.

The remedies are not technically difficult, but they demand a discipline that offices rarely sustain. Records ought to be stored in open, documented formats rather than proprietary ones. They should be migrated to current formats at fixed intervals, whether or not anyone has asked for them. And at least two copies should exist in physically separate buildings, because a single fire or a single failed drive is enough to end a district's memory.

None of this is glamorous work. It produces no visible service and wins no awards. But an administration that cannot read its own past cannot be held accountable for it, and accountability, in the end, is what records are for."

According to the passage, the safety of a paper file traditionally depended on —
options: the quality of the paper used
the diligence of the clerk handling it
the building in which it was stored
the number of copies made
explanation: पहले ही अनुच्छेद में लिखा है: "…its safety depended entirely on the diligence of the clerk who carried it." काग़ज़ की गुणवत्ता, भवन या प्रतियों की संख्या का ज़िक्र वहाँ है ही नहीं।
